claims.text: Introducing a minor alloying addition will improve glass-forming ability in phosphorus-containing high-entropy alloys.
Introducing the same minor alloying addition will improve the thermal stability of the amorphous state.
The target alloys tend to crystallize because they have insufficient chemical disorder.
The alloying addition should be present at up to approximately 5 atomic percent.
A candidate element with significant atomic-size mismatch and strongly negative mixing enthalpy with phosphorus or other constituents will promote the desired effect.
The intervention should work only when the added element does not form its own stable intermetallic phases.
The beneficial effect is confined to an optimal, narrow concentration range.
The addition increases local chemical disorder.
Increased chemical disorder and configurational entropy kinetically frustrate crystalline-phase nucleation.
The added element disrupts regular atomic packing and increases atomic-size mismatch.
Packing disruption and atomic-size mismatch raise the energy barrier for crystallization.
The addition reduces atomic mobility in the undercooled liquid.
Reduced atomic mobility delays crystallization during thermal exposure and stabilizes the amorphous structure.
The modified alloy will have a higher critical casting thickness than the alloy with 0% addition.
The modified alloy will have a higher DSC crystallization-onset temperature than the alloy with 0% addition.
Concentrations outside the beneficial range may provide no improvement or may promote unwanted intermetallic phases.
